Input: When is Putin going to see sense and note that his conventional military forces can’t take Ukraine let alone a NATO member? This question is 2 years and 4 months old: it was asked on April 16, 2022 — less than 2 months after the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In over 2 years, Putin hasn’t figured out that his war is doomed — and keeps destroying Russia, its past, present and future. Russia has lost its reputation of a strong military power, lost hundreds of thousands of men on the battlefield (and millions to emigration), destabilized and cannibalized its economy, wasted enormous human and material resources, got pushed out of its most lucrative international markets, exhausted its already worn out and under-maintained infrastructure, with no ability to afford capital investment. In July 2024, Russia managed to gain more territory (red dots) — and lost 50,000 men doing that. The situation looks even more pointless for Russia if we look at the larger map. In fact, Russia still controls about the same percentage of the Ukrainian territory as in December 2022 — and much less than 2 years ago. Russia’s territorial gains of “800 square km” in 2024, which the Russian ministry of defence brags about, should be viewed to scale — Ukraine is 603,628 square km in size. 800 square km is 0.13%. To gain it, Russia has lost 200,000 men. 2.5 years after the start of the full-scale war, Russia is still unable to gain the full control of Donetsk region — the goal that Putin announced since day 1. 2.5 years!! At this rate, Russia will reach the borders of the Donetsk region in a few decades, having burned down its entire male population. With every month, Russia has to throw in more men than before — but the gains are getting smaller, not bigger. There are many reasons for that, including the quality of new recruits — it dropped substantially since the start of the war, as well as increased sophistication of the warfare — by now, drones became the leading defense tool for Ukraine, and Russia is unable to keep up the pace. The war that Putin refuses to stop is eating Russia from the inside like cancer. The Russian Federation wanted to absorb Ukraine, but in the process started eating itself. If Russia doesn’t lose any of its territories as the result of this war, I’ll be very surprised.

What impact could imprisoned ultranationalist Igor Girkin's political maneuvers have on Russian President Vladimir Putin? Yesterday, the appeal court upheld the verdict of the Moscow City Court against the 53-year-old former commander of pro-Russian separatists in Donetsk Igor Girkin. Girkin (Strelkov), who is a former FSB officer, was arrested a month after the infamous Prigozhin’s coup of June 2023, and charged with “extremism”. While we know there is basically no such thing as “a former FSB officer” (you are always either an asset of the force — or a traitor, sentenced to elimination), for a long time, Girkin’s rants about the sorry state of affairs in the Russian army fighting in Ukraine didn’t cause him any trouble. So much so that most people decided that Girkin-Strelkov had powerful backers among the FSB ranks who were playing their own game. But after Prigozhin’s aborted coup, the rules of the game obviously changed. As soon as Prigozhin and his goons had been removed from the scene and their influence nullified, Girkin (who was actually a fierce opponent of Prigozhin) was arrested and thrown in Lefortovo prison — the same FSB pre-trial jail where recently arrested generals of the ministry of defence are now locked up. In January 2024, Girkin was found guilty and sentenced to 4 years in prison. Girkin’s family members were not allowed into the court during yesterday’s hearing, his wife Miroslava Reginskaya wrote on Telegram. In the near future, Girkin will be transferred to the penal colony. It was previously reported that the ex-separatist leader expressed a desire to join the Russian armed forces and go to the war in Ukraine — the war, which he personally unleashed in 2014. Under the Russian law, those convicted of extremism are not eligible for “conditional release” granted to those who sign the contract with the ministry of defence, to go to the war. Thus, Girkin can only sign an army contract if Vladimir Putin pardons him. Which will never happen — free and unhinged Girkin is a real threat to Putin’s regime, especially with a weapon in his hands. Plus he knows too much and would be a perfect witness for Putin’s Hague trial. And his worst offense, he insulted Putin personally — which makes Girkin a “traitor”, an unforgivable sin in the eyes of vengeful Putin. When his time of release gets near, Girkin will either “suddenly die” or get a new jail term — this time a much longer one. Girkin posted enough to be sentenced for “treason”, “discrediting the army” — or dozens of other offenses, designed by Putin’s regime to lock up the people who cause trouble. Girkin is finished. Anyone who is still supporting him might find themselves in FSB “interview rooms” pretty soon.

Why do you think the Russian government has refused to open a criminal investigation into the death of Alexei Navalny? The Russian state officially announced they wouldn’t be investigating the death of oppositionist Alexei Navalny — naturally, the FSB doesn’t want anyone near the obvious murder case, implicating Putin’s regime. Apparently, Navalny became unwell during his morning walk. He complained of a sharp stomach pain. He was taken back to the solo punishment cell by the guards, where he was thrown for some “violation”. It was the 27th time Navalny was in a solo punishment cell, usually this would be a 14-day punishment. He was found unresponsive in his cell later by guards and taken to medical quarters, an ambulance was called, but couldn’t revive him. A day before his death Navalny participated in a video hearing of his complaint and was in good spirits, appearing healthy. 2 days before his death, his parents visited him in prison, and also reported he was feeling well. The details on the actual circumstances of Navalny’s death were apparently reported by some guards or other prisoners through connections that his friend, investigator Christo Grozev, and other anti-Putin Russians in exile have within the Russian prison system. The papers provided by the Russian investigative committee, refusing to investigate causes of death, say that Navalny was taken to the medics from the walk. The official document also doesn’t mention Navalny’s complaint about the sharp stomach pain. Death was recorded at 2:17 pm. The time of death was recorded at that time, which is already fake, as he had likely died in the cell — he was unconscious when taken to the medical quarters. ”He was dying alone,” said Navalny’s widow Yulia. The cause of death is listed as “the combination of several illnesses”, and the main cause as “arrhythmia” (which is unidentifiable posthumously and never previously was diagnosed). Looks like Navalny might have been poisoned by an unknown toxin. Which probably will be never found, because the family agreed to bury the body. It’s 6 months since the death of Alexei Navalny. The team of investigators, linked to his exiled colleagues, still didn’t post anything conclusive about the causes of his death, but it’s possible they know much more than what his widow Yulia Navalnaya revealed in her yesterday’s video. It’s possible they even know the names of those FSB officers who visited the prison at the time, tasked to kill Navalny.

Is Trump right about negotiating with Putin? “Somebody has to help this country. And if they don’t, the country and the world are in a big trouble. Because in the short period of time, as sure as we are sitting here, there won’t be a country and there won’t be a world.” This tirade is from Donald Trump’s interview circa 1985. (Video in the comments below.) “You said that you could do a better job negotiating an arms control agreement with the Soviets than some of these professionals who’ve been trying to do it for years?” asks the interviewer. “If it were me, it would be fine. I can do it,” states Trump. In 1985, Trump didn’t get a chance to negotiate with the Soviets. So, indeed, there is no such country anymore: in 1991, the USSR ceased to exist. If there are no negotiations with Putin, then the Russian Federation might cease to exist, too. Or, more likely, Putin’s regime will cease to exist first. Meanwhile, residents of Russian town of Belgorod seem to be waking up from the propaganda-induced dream. “Why do we live like this? Why there’s no protection for people? Why don’t we have bomb shelters? Why are we forced to hide in basements? Why are we forced to evacuate somewhere – we don’t even know where, to leave our apartments? Why do they adopt laws about mass burials in peaceful time? What does it mean? What do these laws involve?” asked the delegate from the group that united representatives from several border regions. Belgorod region is under daily strikes from Ukraine, which are targeting military facilities and artillery locations that attack Kharkiv region of Ukraine since February 2022. Belgorod residents don’t want to evacuate because their homes will surely be looted and most likely also destroyed: if people are gone, Russian troops use their homes as fortifications. The speaker continued: “We will demand that those responsible for protecting the population are held accountable. We demand an immediate resignation of the president of the Russian Federation, Putin Vladimir Vladimirovich.” The activists also demanded the governor of Belgorod region to resign and be checked for the crimes of negligence and sabotage. This is very different to regular video appeals that Russians record (usually standing on their knees) begging Putin for help. There were power outages in Belgorod region lately, so the people weren’t getting their regular daily dose of TV propaganda. Maybe that’s the reason why their eyes suddenly opened to the true reasons for their misery?

Why are the Russians targeting residential areas in Ukraine? A captain of a Russian ship confessed targeting residential buildings: “If it’s a 5-storey building, then we aim at the entrance. If it doesn’t hit this one, then it will definitely hit some other building in the neighborhood.” He said the precision of the strikes is “within inches”. So, Russians themselves admit what they are doing. Russian military bloggers reveal why they are doing it: because they want to make Ukrainians surrender, because Russia can’t “win” otherwise. Targeting residential buildings is a completely deliberate strategy. Weirdly, there are still some people in the West buying Russia’s excuses.

Is Europe ready for a new arms race? “It is time for Europe to build a true European Defence Union,” posted Ursula von der Leyen after her re-election as president of the European Commission. Her candidacy was supported by 401 members of the European Parliament (284 members voted against, 15 abstained). Von der Leyen recalled the barbaric attack on the ‘Okhmatdyt’ children’s hospital in Kyiv, saying that “this attack was not a mistake, it was a signal” and stating that Europe’s response must be resolute. “No one wants peace more than Ukraine and the Ukrainian people. A just and sustainable peace for a free and independent country. And Europe will support Ukraine as long as it takes,” she added. Von der Leyen's re-election and her strong attitude show that the Kremlin was unable to split the European Union on the issue of supporting Ukraine. Which is good news.

Does Russia have an "advanced economy"? That’s a major road in Yakutia — an autonomous republic in Siberia, Russia, which is rich in oil, gas, diamonds and gold. (Video in the comments below.) This is where a lot of Russian resources are being extracted from the ground to be sold abroad. Yakutia doesn’t get much back from the Moscow government. Putin continues confiscating large factories and industrial plants from the owners, who got control over former Soviet assets during privatization in 1990s. For 30 years, no one at the top of the Russian state had a problem with the way that Soviet assets had been privatized in 1990s. But Putin began a big war and managed to install a full-on dictatorship in Russia, so he is now confiscating whatever he wishes, stating that the owners either acquired the assets incorrectly, or were not operating them correctly. Russian oligarchs who chose not to make noise when Putin started the war in Ukraine for the fear of losing their assets, and decided not to speak up about the Russian state taking away the remains of citizens’ rights and freedoms, are now losing both their assets and their freedom — literally (the owners are arrested and thrown in jail). In Moscow, 5-star hotel “Four Seasons”, located next to the Kremlin, has just been seized from its owner, 50-year-old Alexei Khotin. Khotin was sentenced to 9 years imprisonment in March 2024. Alexei Khotin is a former owner of Yugra Bank. Since 2022, based on claims from the Prosecutor General’s Office, more than 100 large Russian enterprises have been seized from their owners in favor of the state. The total value of seized assets is 1.3 trillion ruble. Putin claims that the Russian economy is growing, but in fact, officially 1/3 of Russia’s budget is now spent on military expenses. De facto, it’s over 50%, because there are massive expenses on propaganda and also part of the budget is classified (presumed military spending). Military production brings no value to Russia, because everything is shipped to Ukraine, where it’s getting blown into smithereens. It doesn’t create national wealth, nor it improves people’s lives. This is why Russia’s claimed “economic growth” is false — military expenditure (which includes not only the production of weapons, but also the logistics to deliver the weapons to Ukraine) must be deducted from the GDP figure, to understand what is really happening with the Russian economy. Meanwhile, the spending on maintenance and new infrastructure projects in Russia hit record lows, due to the lack of funds — everything is spent on the war. That’s the quality of roads in the vicinity of Siberian cities of Lensk, Mirny, Chernyshevsk and others. During the period when Lena River isn’t under ice, goods are delivered to Lensk by boats. Then trucks transport the goods to populated areas. Meanwhile, the Russian TV happily announced that regular tours to North Korea are now available for Russian tourists. Important guests from Taliban were begged to attend the “International Economic Forum” in St. Petersburg (probably, paid to come). After attending the forum on economics, the Taliban reps will fly to Kazan, Russia, to share their experience in the field of education at the forum “Shaping the Future”. The Taliban who banned girls from going to school, women from teaching at universities — or even getting outside their homes without a burqa, and where women can be publicly stoned to death. 20 years ago, I would have never believed that Russians would admire and sing praises to the North Korea, Iranian ayatollahs, Yemeni Houthis and the Taliban. But we have what we have. And Russians don’t even find it weird.

Why do Russians put up with Putin? Vladimir Putin was appointed the Chairman of the Government of the Russian Federation in August 1999 — a quarter of a century ago. 4 months later, Russian President Boris Yeltsin officially resigned, leaving Putin in charge of Russia. It was Yeltsin’s “Family” — his daughter, her husband, and his neo-oligarch friends — who picked a “no-name” ex-KGB clerk to rule Russia, in exchange to guarantees of personal safety and protection of their wealth — acquired during privatization of the USSR assets during 1990s (effectively, stolen from the Soviet people). Daughter of the first Russian president Tatyana Dyachenko and her husband Valentin Yumashev, head of Yeltsin’s presidential administration. Putin agreed to all “conditions” when he came to power — and immediately began enriching himself and his own friends. But Putin used his KGB training. KGB operatives are trained to always hide their plans and never tell the truth. So, Putin was always telling the Russian people what they wanted to hear, gave strong promises he never intended to keep, and concealed what he was actually doing. Putin put personal loyalty to him over professionalism and ability, removed anyone smart and capable from leadership positions, dismantled the free media and liquidated — one by one — all his opponents. The ex-Soviet people, who never actually learned critical thinking and never acquired self-respect and dignity during the short pseudo-democratic period of 1989–1999 — shadowed by the hyper-inflation unleashed by the ex-communists who retained the power, who needed the economic collapse to steal the Soviet assets from the people, causing mass poverty and suffering, amidst the background of mushrooming crime and gang wars stemming from the Soviet exit from Afghanistan and return of combatants who found themselves not needed and without means in the fast-changing reality of collapsing communism — so, these ex-Soviet people, exhausted by the decade of “pseudo-democracy”, were ecstatic to relax back into the reality where someone else was making decisions for them. Putin started his work at the helm of the Russian government by making himself known and visible: he ordered the FSB to bomb apartment towers in Moscow, Buynaksk, and Volgodonsk, which killed 300 people — but terrified all 146 million of Russian citizens. “Chechen terrorists” were blamed, and Putin began the Second Chechen war. Putin rules through lies, war and terror. He is a murderer and a thief who was given a giant country to rule, and he turned it into a mafia state — in accordance with his upbringing by a criminal boss, who happened to be his first judo trainer. It was that mafia boss that told him to go to a KGB school. Putin as a teenager. After becoming the president of Russia, he made his childhood friends billionaires, in exchange to unconditional loyalty. “Traitors” were mercilessly executed. A sadistic psychopath, trained by the mafia and KGB, put at the helm of the largest country in the world, what could go wrong? The Soviet people, after 70 years of communism, shaped by Stalin’s purges that liquidated anyone with intelligence, initiative and pride, and 2 world wars, where people were sent into never-ending slaughter of meat attacks, shaped by famines, repressions and totalitarian propaganda, were pliable, bred by the tyrannical regime for compliance and obedience. And that obedience takes roots in the centuries when Muscovy was part of the Mongol empire, and Russian princes were vassals of Mongol Khans. And then the Muscovy princes pushed away the Khans — and became just as ruthless rulers themselves. That innate obedience takes roots in the Russian slavery — noblemen owned peasants until 1861. The owners could do anything they wanted with the serfs, from raping virgins prior to giving them into marriage (at the age of 12–13) — the owner could pick the groom he preferred or allow the slave’s parents to pick one, to using girls for his unofficial harem (as servants in the estate). From casual beatings for various offenses (many had been beaten to death), to selling them to another owner, separating families, just on a whim. Slave peasants weren’t paid, they were working for food and shelter (the nobleman owned the land where they lived). The majority of Russian people never learned critical thinking, dignity and self-respect. They exist in the environment ruled by a tyranny of the state, permeated by state propaganda, corruption and unfairness. They exist, survive and endure — they don’t “live” in the true meaning of that word.

What are the impacts of the fires at the Proletarsk oil depot in Russia on the environment? The fire at the strategic oil depot in the ARussian town of Proletarsk in Rostov region has been burning for 9 days, and almost all fuel had burnt out. (Video in the comments below.) But despite the smoke tail of 60 km long, the local enviromental control authorities assured residents that the quality of air was fine. Notwithstanding, the annual celebration of the Day of the City got cancelled by the administration, as well as all other outdoor activities — even though it’s the 100-year-anniversary of the district. The district administration's press service stated that the festivities were cancelled due to "the current situation in the district." (“The situation” is also the word used by Vladimir Putin to describe the Ukrainian invasion of Russia in the Kursk region.) Residents of Proletarsk complain that they have "no air to breathe" and are buying up masks to breathe filtered air. Locals are afraid to eat the vegies from their gardens: when they wash them, the water turns black. Compared to the first week of the fire, it looks like the flames are getting smaller, expectedly, as not much fuel is left. The fire began as the result of the Ukrainian drone attack on August 18. After 4 days, the local authorities even called priests to perform a prayer service, asking for divine assistance in putting out the flames. The prayers didn’t work; attempts to control the fire by firemen also didn’t work. Over 40 firemen got injured. The fuel depot had 74 giant tanks storing different types of fuel, including specific types of aviation kerosine. Russia’s ministry of emergency situations that controls the fire service didn’t post any information about the raging fire in Proletarsk, which was visible on satellite photos. The reason for the silence — not to give information to the Ukrainian Telegram channels, which would celebrate their success. At the beginning of the war, it was Russia that was destroying oil depots in Ukraine with missile strikes. Ukraine is simply paying back.

Is it true that all of Russia is built on lies and deception? Vadim Krasikov, who was imprisoned in Germany for a murder of a former Chechen rebel leader in Berlin, worked for the Russian security service FSB, Putin admits. He previously denied this. Apparently, Vadim Krasikov’s connection to Vladimir Putin goes back to 1990’s when he was a bodyguard for Putin during his time as Sobchak’s aide. Some even say that it was Krasikov who is responsible for Sobchak’s assassination in February 2000 after his return to Russia. After Putin failed to get Sobchak re-elected as the mayor of St. Petersburg in 1996 (Putin was the chief of his election campaign), the ex-mayor had an economic crimes investigative commission after him and emigrated to avoid prosecution for corruption and theft. Anatoly Sobchak with his aide Vladimir Putin. Sobchak lived in France since 1997 and returned only in July 1999 — 2 weeks before Boris Yeltsin officially appointed Putin as the head of the government (it was by then obviously a done deal). It was Yeltsin’s “Family” — his daughter Tatyana, her husband Valentin Yumashev and his oligarch friends — who actually were responsible for the selection of Yeltsin’s successor. They picked Putin because he promised them to keep the “Family” free from prosecution for any misdeeds and allow them to keep the wealth they seized when the USSR state assets were stolen from the people in 1990s. Sobchak’s daughter Ksenia made a film “The Case” (“Delo Sobchaka”) in 2018 that depicts how Putin organized a “special operation” to allow Sobchak to emigrate to avoid prosecution: officially he left to get a treatment for ill health. Reportedly, when Anatoly Sobchak was told for the first time that his former aide would become a president of Russia, he found the idea hilarious: the ex-mayor of St. Petersburg didn’t believe that Putin was fit for the job. So, after he was lured to return to Russia, Anatoly Sobchak died within months — before Putin’s official election as the president in March 2000. In her book “The Man Without a Face: The Unlikely Rise of Vladimir Putin”, journalist Masha Gessen claimed that Anatoly Sobchak was killed by placing a poison (specially designed by KGB to cause death that appears natural), on a night light by his bed. One version why Putin had such an urgent need to free Krasikov from a German prison is that Putin feared that Krasikov could make a deal with the German authorities and reveal over time some information that would be extremely harmful to the Kremlin. Krasikov was so important for Putin that he gave 12 Russian political prisoners to get him back. Vadim Krasikov became the only man among the released Russian agents whom Putin not only shook hands with, but also publicly hugged. Putin also admitted that Krasikov was an FSB officer, which he previously denied. Kremlin bots now threaten that any Putin’s enemies who live abroad could be killed by Russian assassins and call Krasikov a “hero” and a “true patriot”. That’s the whole Kremlin propaganda campaign around the latest Russian-Western prisoner exchange deal.

What do you think about Bellingcat's analysis that the missile that hit Okhmatdyt Children's Hospital in Kyiv was a Kh-101 missile? Bellingcat has one of the most thorough and methodical investigative teams. It were them who found a guy responsible for the poisoning of Alexei Navalny — Bellingcat managed to find his mobile phone number and cleverly dropped enough details of the crime that convinced the culprit to confess over the phone. It was the Bellingcat team who found a link between the trips of Russian GRU agents from the “assassin team” and episodes of “Havana Syndrome” among employees of the USA embassies around the world. On July 9, 2024, Bellingcat released their report on identifying the missile that hit the largest Ukrainian children’s hospital ‘Okhmatdyt’ on July 8 concluding with certainty — including the geolocated images — that it was a Russian Kh-101 missile that deliberately targeted the civilian medical facility, debunking Russia’s claim that it was a Norway-supplied air defense missile. Woefully for Russia, the moment of a strike was captured by a Ukrainian onlooker on video, showing the arrival of the missile and the sound accompanying it. An enhanced image showing the missile that hit the children’s hospital in Kyiv. Several international military experts identified the missile as Kh-101 that only Russia uses. Although the Ukrainian side only released the images of the parts of the missile, found in the rubble, Bellingcat researchers found a photo taken by a journalist at the site that matches the photos of the missile wreckage released by the Ukrainian side. But the most profound admission of Russia’s guilt came from none other as the UN rep for RF, Vasily Nebenzya. Without lifting eyes from the paper in front of him, Nebenzya proclaimed that if it were indeed a Russian missile that hit Okhmatdyt, “nothing would have remained of the building, and all the people in it would have died.” It’s a blatant and moronic lie. Nebenzya cannot not know that — he denied Russia’s strikes on civilian targets many times before — and still, he duly reads the lies that are given to him. This moronic lie is yet another proof that it was Russia that hit the children’s hospital — and they targeted the medical clinic for seriously sick kids deliberately.

What is your analysis of the satellite images of the Ukrainian Defence Intelligence drone strikes on the Russian radar station in Orenburg Oblast? On May 26, a long-range Ukrainian drone attacked an over-the-horizon radar station in Russia in Orenburg region — at a distance of more than 1,800 km. Orsk is located 140 km further from the front line in Ukraine than the Bashkir city of Salavat, which was previously the furthest location from Ukraine attacked by Ukrainian drones in Russia. The drone targeted the Voronezh-M missile attack warning radar station in the village of Gorkovskoye near the town of Orsk in Orenburg region. The station is fairly new — it was commissioned in 2017. 2 days ago, Ukraine already hit another Voronezh-DM radar station, located in the Krasnodar Territory. “Voronezh” type stations are designed to detect and track ballistic and cruise missiles and other aerodynamic objects at distances up to 6,000 These long-range radar stations are part of Russia’s “strategic umbrella”. Since 2011, these radar stations became part of Russia’s Aerospace Defense Forces. It is these stations that Russia is using to hit targets in Ukraine. Like the attack on Kharkiv hypermarket last Saturday.

Has the surprise Ukrainian incursion caused chaos in the Kursk region? The residents of territories taken over by the Ukrainian troops in the Kursk region are terrified and bitter, and warn Russians to don’t believe anything they see on TV (video in the comments below). The administration and government services were the first to run away, often leaving documentation behind. In the local police, folders with criminal cases against local residents who escaped military enlistment were left behind — the Ukrainian soldiers burned them. Avoiding mobilization is a crime punishable by 10 years in prison in Russia. Ukrainian forces knocked out the last remaining bridge over the Seim river, destroying 3 out of 3 bridges connecting the area with the rest of the Kursk region — practucally cutting off the Glushkovsky district: a 700 square km triangle has the Ukrainian border on one side, Ukrainian troops on the other side, and river on the third side. Reportedly, around 2,700 Russian soldiers and officers are now cut off on that territory. In social networks, locals are looking for dinghies and blow up boats, to enable them to cross the Seim River. “Don’t believe what they say on TV,” urge Sudzha residents their compatriots, adding that “no one is telling the truth.” Despite the Russian media giving a heavily moderated version of “events in the Kursk region” (Putin called it “a situation”), Muscovites are starting to get worried. “Guys, honestly I've been scared this whole week. I'm scared that my house will be destroyed, I'm in shock. Kursk region is 500 km from Moscow. And how do people with children live? Are they doubly scared? I don't know what to do, I'm a coward and a nervous wreck,” writes one girl. ”Let our Crimea become a grave for you. For you and other occupiers. May all of you die for this Ukrainian peninsula that you needed so much. I won't even mention the tens of thousands of kilometers of scorched earth. Stock up on gloves — you'll need them to clear the rubble at home and for digging out your neighbors. Greetings from Donetsk,” responded a Ukrainian who had to run away from the Russian occupation twice — in 2014 from Donetsk and in 2022 from the Kyiv region. Washington Post reporters visited Sudzha and talked to a dozen of locals. Sudzha residents said that they have been treated well by the Ukrainian soldiers and do not know of any residents killed. But they still want things to be back as they were. Despite them living right next to the border and the war with Ukraine raging for over 2.5 years, they never thought it would reach them. One man said he wants Putin to come to an agreement with Zelenskyy, so that “everything is resolved in a good way”. One man said he wanted to find his daughter in Kharkiv (Ukraine), whom he couldn’t see since the start of the war. “We want peace and harmony. We don't want anything else; we don't care for anything else,” said another woman. “Please help us,” she begged WP reporters. “But we are just civilians,” kept saying Sudzha residents. So were the Ukrainians who live under Russian bombs and missiles for 2.5 years. No place in Ukraine is safe — nowhere in the whole of Ukraine. Russia can hit any town or village with their long-range missiles and drones. Sudzha residents asked reporters to send photos of the destroyed buildings in their town to Vladimir Putin. They still believe that he would help them. Not sure if the reporters told them that Putin is too busy — he’s laying wreaths in Baku, Azerbaijan, and dining with the country’s ruler and his wife, thousands of miles from the Kursk region.

Should Ukraine be allowed use American weapons to hit targets in Russia? TAP ON THE PHOTO TO VIEW. Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told the media that weapons from the United States and other Western countries supplied to Ukraine are already hitting targets in Russia. “We proceed from the fact that American and other Western weapons are hitting targets on Russian territory,” said Lavrov. Great point Lavrov! If Russia thinks this, then clearly it’s not a problem. No “red lines” whatsoever. Great job Lavrov.

How come Russians still cannot see they are such a pathetic laughing stock and everybody looks down on them? Why can't Russians still see that living under the boot of psychopaths is very embarrassing? Pavel Guguev (left), a Russian soldier who returned back to Russia after a prisoner exchange, was imprisoned on his return home – in the best Stalin’s traditions. Like many Russians, Pavel Guguev was recruited for the war from prison. In fact, Russians are shutting down several prisons, because they cleaned up the population of inmates by sending them to the war. Vsevolod Vukolov. Coming back to Guguev’s story, by 2022, he served 10 out of 12 years of his sentence for murder, but when recruiters from the ministry of defence came to his prison, he decided to sign up “to defend the homeland”. Little he knew that “Storm-Z” units, where prisoners were sent, only needed convicts as cheap consumables that could be sent to reconnoiter the firing points of the Ukrainians. This is what happened with the detachment of disposable soldiers in which Guguev was. He was lucky to survive — he got captured by the Ukrainian troops. When he was in Ukrainian captivity, Guguev gave an interview to journalist Dmitry Karpenko (right). Karpenko and another Ukrainian journalist, Volodymyr Zolkin, began interviewing captured Russian soldiers from the first weeks of the Russian invasion of Ukraine. They published videos on YouTube, hoping that the truth told by the Russian soldiers would help to stop the war quickly. That hope was in vain: despite the interviews scoring millions of views, it didn’t help to turn the public opinion in Russia against the war. Vice versus, the voices of dissent in Russia, quite loud at the start of the war, all but disappeared by now, with anyone speaking against the war immediately detained by the FSB. Like the vast majority of captured prisoners, Guguev openly spoke to Ukrainian journalists about the realities of his military service in the ranks of the Russian Army, the huge losses, and the attitude of commanders towards the soldiers. On June 11, 2023, Guguev returned to Russia after a prisoners exchange. But instead of going home, he and other returning Russian POWs were locked up in the barracks of a military unit in Moscow region. For over a month, the returned soldiers were interrogated by the FSB, assigned the status of “untrustworthy”, refused proper medical care, weren’t given an opportunity to see their families. Locked in the army barracks with other returned POWs, Guguev again talked to journalist Dmitry Karpenko via a mobile phone, telling him of their plight. He also told: Guguev compared how the Ukrainians treated him in captivity with the conditions of detention in Russia. Immediately after the interview was published, he was arrested and a criminal case was opened against him. Those Russians who dare to tell the truth are imprisoned, killed, branded traitors and forced out of the country. Every authoritarian regime is built on lies and hiding the truth. Russian opposition politicians were the first victims in the fight against the truth, then the regime began arresting journalists, prosecuting ordinary Russians who spoke against Putin and his war. Now, the regime is attacking anyone who dares to speak up: As long as they die quietly and agree to all the Kremlin’s policies, they are “heroes.” But as soon as they start telling the truth, describe the facts of reality, the proven Stalin’s principle is used: “No person, no problem.”

How do Russian pilots drop glide bombs? Russian military correspondents confirmed that the Russian pilots are dropping glide bombs on Russian towns in the Kursk region, which are under control of the Ukrainian armed forces. According to Z-correspondents, “the order has been confirmed at the very top.” The same pilots who bombed with glide bombs Ukrainian Bakhmut and Vovchansk are now bombing the Russian towns near the border, on orders of the Russian generals. The population of the territories under control of the Ukrainian Armed Forces and their property have been already written off by Putin. Putin ordered to pay each refugee 10,000 ruble (USD $115). Generous offer in the usual Putin’s style. To get this generous payout, one only needs to gather proper documentation on the lost property: compile an inventory, confirm the losses with documents, and get an official valuation. Just over 10 certificates — and to get some of these papers, one has to pay a fee. And only those whose registered place of residence was destroyed, only they can get $115 — and only for 1 property, not for all the houses they might own. That is, you are a refugee, you had to escape in a hurry, leaving everything behind — and the officials demand that you confirm that you are from there and owned the property that you lost, for $100 of Putin's aid. No doubt, the local and Moscow officials will steal most of the allocated funds. It’s Russia, after all.

What are some positive aspects of Russian culture and its people? Russian military correspondents are furious: residents of Kursk region are evacuating, instead of queuing to sign up as volunteers for the Russian army. (Video in the comments below.) “What the heck??” barks a Russian man dressed in a military uniform. “As males, you should be defending your homes, you should be delivering food to our guys, or digging trenches — or if you can’t do it, just give your cars to our guys, so they can use them at the front. Why are you just driving away??” For 25 years, since Putin took helm in Russia, the state was training citizens to be passive: “They at the top know best what to do”, “we are just small people”, “we can’t change anything”. People have learned to don’t have any opinions of their own, because having an opinion can get you in trouble. They’ve learned to “stay out of politics”, learned to live by the motto, “my hut is at the edge of the village, I don’t know anything”. Putin’s administration chose to downplay “the situation in Kursk region” and Russian propagandists are now saying that “Ukraine made a foolish move” and “everything is under control, situation stabilized, no losses.” Kursk residents know it’s not true — they can look out of the window and see what happens, but because the state tells them “it’s all good”, they simply do what they feel is the right thing for them — run away. They don’t want to defend Putin’s regime, they don’t want to fight and possibly die defending their homeland. It’s weird, but there are no public protests in Russian towns taken over by the Ukrainian forces, as there were in spring 2022 when the Russian army invaded Ukrainian cities and thousands of Ukrainians went to town squares to protest against the Russian invaders — Ukrainian men, women, elders, kids were standing with bare hands against armed Russian soldiers, yelling at them, “Go home!!” “Occupiers, go home!” — protests in Kherson in March 2022. Similar mass protests were happening in many other Ukrainian towns captured by the Russian army. People in Kherson were standing with Ukrainian flags, with anti-Putin and anti-Russia posters, against armed Russians and military vehicles. Russians don’t protest. They seem to be indifferent to what is happening around them. They realized their officials lie to them — they knew it all along, but it was safer to pretend they believed them — and they have no idea what is real and what is not anymore, they just don’t trust anybody — but pretend to trust the guys who are in charge right now. If Ukrainians are in charge, they pretend to trust Ukrainians. If Russians are in charge, they pretend to trust Russians. Russian citizens have no opinions of their own — or if they do, they keep them buried so deep, they themselves are terrified to admit they have them. It’s not a “slave mentality” — it’s learned helplessness. They really think there is nothing they can do that will change anything. Obviously, this aspect of the modern Russian culture and collective psyche is highly beneficial to the advancing Ukrainian army, which doesn’t have to deal with hostile population. Rather, Ukrainians are dealing with passive, yet quietly curious population, compliant and eager to follow instructions. Russian State Duma member Vitaly Milonov called on men from the Kursk region to sign contracts with the Ministry of Defense and defend their homeland on their own — obviously, Putin isn’t going to send to Kursk reinforcements from the front in Ukraine, where he’s sending most troops and equipment. Milonov, too, believes that only women, children and the elderly should be evacuating from Kursk, but local men should take on the defense of border areas. “No one has to do anything for Russian residents of border regions,” announced Milonov — they themselves must show that they can defend their land. With such an attitude from the Russian state, no wonder that Ukrainians keep taking over several more settlements every day. Isn’t it weird that Russians are willing to go to Ukraine “to make Russia great again” (and be paid “big wages”) — but have no desire or interest to defend their own homes?

What is happening in the Kursk region of Russia? In the Kursk region of Russia, which Ukrainian army invaded on August 6, things are moving fast. Ukraine already controls 100 settlements and the territory of 1,300 km², reported commander-in-chief Syrskyi. Time to let Ukraine take Russia! Russian military bloggers say that Ukrainian forces broke through defenses in Belgorod region — that’s the second Russian region getting invaded. Meanwhile, Russian volunteers who arrived to Kursk region with “humanitarian aid” for the Russian army (food, water, socks and jocks for soldiers, because the Russian army doesn’t provide for its troops — officers steal all the money) — so, these “volunteers” complain about traffic police cameras, which continue to send them tickets for speeding — while they are driving over the speed limits to avoid drones or shelling. The traffic police office responded that “war is war, but a violation is a violation” and fines that have already been issued in the system can only be challenged in court. You know, in Russia the law is the law! (Unless, of course, you are above the law, in which case you can break any laws you want.) I suppose, the Ukrainian tanks must have scored hundreds of fines for illegal parking. The new map of Eastern Europe has just been leaked on Telegram. On 24 February 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, the world was discussing how long Ukraine would be able to withstand against Russia — 2 days, 3 days, a week? Not many gave Ukraine more than 2 weeks. On August 6, 2024, when Ukraine invaded the Kursk region of Russia, Vladimir Putin ordered “to squeeze the enemy out”. On day 3, the chief of Russian general staff Gerasimov reported to Putin that the enemy had been repelled and destroyed. That was more than 3 weeks ago. Ukrainians are still in the Kursk region and keep increasing their stronghold. And now , Russians are told by their TV channels that "The incursion into Kursk region by the Ukrainians is beneficial to Russia, because it closes the conversations about negotiations with Ukraine.” Putin hopes that “the situation” in the Kursk region will somehow sort itself out, so he tries not to make a big deal about “mighty Russia” getting invaded by a “little, insignificant Ukraine.” Being invaded by a foreign power is Russia’s “new normal”.

What would make people laugh at Putin? Putin’s claims about Russia’s economic “progress” are the butt of many jokes. Yesterday, at St. Petersburg’s international economic forum, Putin announced that Russia has already overtaken Japan and Germany in terms of the size of the economy, but it needs to ensure stable growth further. “Literally last week, the World Bank made additional calculations and put Russia in 4th place,” Putin announced proudly. “Russia has the fourth largest GDP in terms of purchasing power parity, as I said, ahead of Japan,” insisted Putin. I don’t know what numbers Rosstat supplies to the World Bank (the World Bank uses the official Russian statistics), but 80% of Russia looks like this: I don’t believe for a second that a Japanese worker earning the average wage can buy less food or things than someone earning the average wage in Russia. Maybe, only if they calculate how many loafs of bread one can buy (bread only), but not if you compare the actual needs of a person living a regular life. For Russians, the lifestyle of an average Japanese is the level of unaffordable luxury. Meanwhile, in the center of Moscow, on Bobrov Lane, an elevator fell out of a shaft. Just by pure luck, a person didn’t end up dead. Soon there could be many more such incidents. The Russian authorities decided to increase the service life of dilapidated lifts from 25 to 30 years. 70,000 elevators in Russia (Russia doesn’t produce lifts but had been buying them abroad all these years) are at the end of their service life. Maintenance is also an issue because of western sanctions. At the same time, the level of cajolery towards Putin is hitting record heights. At the SPIEF, the moderator of Putin’s Q&A session promoted him as a messiah whose job is “to save the world,” depicting his appointment in 1999 as an act of “God’s mercy” to Russia. Putin’s face was glowing with delight. If what Russia turned into by 2024 is an act of “God’s mercy”, I am scared to think what God’s wrath towards Russia would look like.

Are Russians surprised that they didn't take Kyiv "in three days"? There were countless statements by Russian propagandists that “taking Kyiv will only take 2–3 days”. Even Belarus leader Alexander Lukashenko made such a statement. In March 2022, Putin himself ensured Russians that “there will be no need for mobilization” — only to announce mobilization 6 months later. So, yes, Russians indeed were expecting that their troops will just march on Kyiv and have a parade in the afternoon. The coping strategy of Russian propagandists is to claim that: The current slogan on billboards in Russia, “Our victory is inevitable.” I’d like to see how Russian propagandists will explain it when Russia loses Crimea and Donbas. Probably, they will say that NATO tried to liquidate Russia as a state, but Russia managed to remain on the globe, and therefore it won.

What do you think will happen to Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich who was arrested for alleged spying in Russia? On July 19, 2024, the Regional Court in Yekaterinburg, Russia, sentenced American journalist Evan Gershkovich to 16 years in a maximum security colony. Russian human rights activist Vladimir Osechkin says that possibly he was baited by the FSB, to facilitate his arrest. 32-year-old journalist of WSJ was found guilty of espionage for collecting information about ‘Uralvagonzavod’, which is a factory that makes tanks for the Russian army. The prosecutor asked for an 18-year sentence. Gershkovich pleaded “not guilty” and insisted that he was acting as a journalist, not a spy. The court hearings were held behind closed doors, as the prosecution alleged the information that Gershkovich was getting was a “state secret”. Only the judge, the prosecutor, the defendant and his lawyers were present. Journalists were allowed into the meeting room for a few minutes before the hearing commenced to take photos and videos. Gershkovich, with a shaved head, greeted his colleagues with a smile, but did not answer any questions. Journalists were also allowed into the courtroom for the announcement of the harsh verdict: 16 years in a maximum security prison. Evan Gershkovich was detained on March 29, 2023 in Yekaterinburg, where he arrived for the second time in a month, to continue his investigation for the next story. At the WSJ Gershkovich worked since January 2022 — he joined the respected media just a month before Russia invaded Ukraine. Since then, he authored several key news stories related to Russia and Ukraine. In early March 2023, weeks before his arrest in Russia, he and his colleagues released a story about the growing tensions between the founder of “Wagner” Yevgeny Prigozhin and the Kremlin elites. In particular, the material stated, Kremlin officials turned to Russian President Vladimir Putin with a request to “rein in” Prigozhin, who criticized the Russian Ministry of Defense. Gershkovich was also one of the authors of a high-profile WSJ article about how Putin’s entourage may be hiding truthful information from him about the war in Ukraine. Putin receives a written report from the front every morning, however, the reports emphasize Russia army’s successes, and failures are tuned down. The reports are also delayed for several days, because they have to pass filters of the FSB and the Security Council, as well as get a personal stamp of approval from Nikolai Patrushev (then the secretary of Russia’s Security Council), the article claimed. Gershkovich's materials before his arrest in March 2023 were devoted to the worsening prospects for the Russian economy, the situation around Bakhmut, the visit to Moscow of China’s leader Xi Jinping and protests over the bill on "foreign agents" in Georgia. According to the photographer who worked with Gershkovich, he was collecting material for an article about how people in Russian regions perceive the war, for which he visited Yekaterinburg and Nizhny Tagil, and planned to go to other cities. The media wrote that Gershkovich was also interested in activities of the “Wagner”, including recruitment and cemeteries of the deceased fighters. At his court process, Gershkovich did not admit guilt and insisted that his research was purely journalistic. Evan Gershkovich became the first American journalist in modern Russian history to be accused of espionage. The last time an American journalist had been detained in Russia on espionage charges was in 1986, when a “News & World Report” employee Nicholas Daniloff was arrested. Daniloff was exchanged 3 weeks later. Before his arrest, Gershkovich worked in Russia for about 6 years, since 2017. At the time of his detainment, he had been living in London but regularly traveled on business trips to Russia, where he worked as part of the WSJ's Moscow bureau. His parents Mikhail Gershkovich and Emma Milman were emigrants from the USSR, but Evan himself lived his entire life in America. Several journalists who were friends with Gershkovich said that they warned him that reporting in Russia on the topics he was picking was dangerous and he could be arrested. But obviously, he didn’t think so. Gershkovich’s name has been frequently mentioned as someone who could be exchanged to Russian spies and assassins, arrested in Europe and the USA. He is probably the highest profile American hostage held by Putin. Putin discussed exchanging Gershkovich in his interview to Tucker Carlson in February 2024. Putin wanted to get in exchange the FSB assassin Vadim Krasikov, who is imprisoned in Germany. In 2021, Vadim Krasikov was sentenced to life in prison for the murder of Chechen field commander Zelimkhan Khangoshvili in Berlin in 2019. Carlson said at the time that Putin needed to talk to Germans about it. Peculiarly, Gershkovich’s process wasn’t held in Moscow but 2 thousand kilometers away, in Yekaterinburg, where he was arrested — away from Russia’s capital, where most of the foreign correspondents reside. This obviously prevented many western ambassadors and embassy officials from attending the process, which they would likely do as a show of solidarity, if the court hearing was in Moscow. The only hope for Gershkovich to get out of the Russian prison is an agreement for an exchange, which Putin would probably only approve if his assassin Krasikov is released, and Germany doesn’t seem keen on that. Otherwise, Gershkovich may only hope to get out if Vladimir Putin, on whose order he was arrested (no doubt, such high profile arrest and prosecution would require the highest nod), is no longer the ruler of Russia. So, Gershkovich is likely to remain behind bars in Russia, as the locals call it, “for as long as Putin is alive.”

How does Russia use social media as a strategy? In an interview on Russian TV, Margarita Simonyan confessed that “Russia Today” is creating 1000’s of fake accounts, to spread disinformation. (Video in the comments below.) In February 2023, in the interview with Boris Korchevnikov for his program “Life and Destiny”, editor-in-chief of ‘RT’ spilled the beans about something, which, in Simonyan’s own admission, she “shouldn’t be talking about”: “It’s best for me not to talk about it… But I will say it bluntly: we create a large number of informational sources, which are not linked to us. And while the CIA investigates and uncovers that they are linked to us, they already have a giant audience. Sometimes they uncover that, shut them down. Sometimes, you wake up in the morning and 600 of your channels have been shut down. But while they are shutting them down, we have already created new ones. So, we are in this race, running after each other. It’s even fun,” Simonyan smirked. “Russia Today” is just one Russian propaganda outlet that uses social media as a strategy. They are oriented on foreigners. The fake accounts created by Russian propaganda outlets are supporting real media personalities, expressing pro-Putin views in the western informational space. I don’t even need to name the names here, we all know who they are. These personalities are paid by entities established by individuals linked to the Russian state and siphoning Russian money to them via a chain of offshore companies and funds. On the lowest level, coordinators from the Russian disinformation departments are hiring commentators from poor countries (including Russia, as well as countries of Asia and Africa), whose job are likes and dislikes, views, and comments under certain posts or accounts. These commentators are hired through online “tasks” websites and paid a few cents per “task”. To earn $10, the commentators likely need to “work” for several hours, but kids and elders with nothing to do are happy to get a few bucks without needing to get off the couch. Thus the poor quality of the majority of pro-Russia comments. There are dozens of such websites with digital tasks. In addition, automated bot accounts ran by software are used to artificially increase the number of likes and views. The Russian state is working very hard to defeat the West. And if Russia’s successes on the battlefield in Ukraine are highly questionable, the Russian propaganda is a mighty enemy that needs to be taken seriously. Just as seriously as the Russian bombs.

Has Putin already decided to attack NATO? Putin can’t attack NATO countries while he’s stuck in the war of attrition in Ukraine. But if Putin is allowed to take over Ukraine — or “freeze” the war on current separation lines, with Ukraine being forced to de-arm and the ability of Russia to mobilize soldiers from the occupied Ukrainian territories (which they already do), then the chance of Putin attacking Baltics increases tenfold. And vice versus, if Russia is decisively defeated in Ukraine, the threat of Putin attacking a NATO country in Europe will drop close to 0%. Russia will not be able to recover quickly and Europe will have enough time to prepare an impenetrable defense. Putin won’t have the resources to attack the Baltic countries or Poland, if he suffers defeat and his army is destroyed in Ukraine. That’s why the most logical course of action for the European allies of Ukraine is to send Ukrainians enough weapons to destroy Putin’s army in Ukraine, so he cannot even think about an attack on Europe. Then these weapons that are stored in the warehouses won’t be needed in the future.

What do you think about the Russian disinformation campaign aimed at undermining the Paris Olympics? Today, Russian media is awash with criticism of Paris Olympics opening ceremony. By the way, Putin banned Russians from watching the 2024 Olympics — because the Olympic committee banned the Russian team from participating under the national flag (only 15 individual athletes with Russian citizenship, who haven’t been not noticed in condoning the war in Ukraine, were allowed to take part in a neutral status). So, why do Russians even bother commenting on something they are not participating in — and haven’t even been allowed to watch by their leaders? "Hellish bad taste" — this is how the known FSB asset Kseniya Sobchak commented on the opening ceremony of Paris Olympics. In the photo: paragon of taste and traditional values K. Sobchak. (Search “Sobchak December 2023 Ivleeva party” for unabridged version.) What is most ridiculous, it’s the people who dress up kids in military garb and turn baby strollers into tanks — and even put fake “Iskander missiles” on top of rusty cars calling to “nuke Washington!” — so, it’s these people who criticize the opening ceremony of Paris Olympics. I guess, the GRU is just furious that their plot to disrupt the opening ceremony in Paris didn’t work out and their guy got arrested just a few days before the event — so, they weren’t even able to plan something else. The Kremlin granddad must be apoplectic. Someone in the GRU might get arrested “for corruption” — that’s the new trendy punishment for those disappointing the tiny tyrant.

Can Ukraine make its own weapons? Ukraine can and does make its own weapons: Russia-Ukraine war of 2022–2024 is the first war in history where drones became the weapons that dominate the terrain. Within the last 2 years, drone production in Ukraine grew 100-fold. Since February 2022, Ukraine created and developed the UAV market from the ground up. One of such manufacturers are making drones called “Hornets”. There are smaller and larger FPV drones — “Wild Hornets”, “Queen Hornets”, as well as other models. All of them are Ukrainian-made. The Ukrainian drone operators have learned to use the same drone for many missions — a drone drops explosives and returns to the base, to get munitions. Drones are even used to retrieve weapons from the battlefield. Here you can see “Hornet Queen” picking weapons on the battlefield using a magnet. In December 2023, Ukraine’s President Zelenskyy set the task of producing a million drones for the Ukrainian Armed Forces. By now, the task has been completed, says Ukraine’s minister of digital transformation Mykhailo Fedorov. There are already contracts for the production of a million of drones for the Ukrainian army. They include standard FPV drones, long-range, reconnaissance and other types of drones that are already used by the Ukrainian defenders at the front. Just imagine this number: 1,000,000 drones! It’s 2 drones per each Russian soldier on the Ukrainian land. But tens of thousands of drones go directly from manufacturers to the Ukrainian units at the front without involving the government and the ministry of defense. They are paid for from donations that people make on behalf of certain units. So, if a certain unit requires more drones, they place a request with a manufacturer they know, and get a delivery within days, without the need for ministerial approvals. This is why the Ukrainian army is so much more efficient, and why the Russian soldiers say that it feels like the Ukrainians have 50:1 advantage in drones. This also saves thousands of Ukrainian lives.

Is Putin a threat to Eastern Europe? Putin is a huge threat to Eastern Europe — that’s why Baltic and most Eastern European countries are the biggest supporters of Ukraine’s fight against the Russian invasion. If Putin’s plans were limited to Ukraine, he wouldn’t have tried to blackmail NATO, demanding the alliance to withdraw to pre-1997 borders in December 2021. The pompous ultimatum was made by Putin, so he could use it as a formal pretext to invade all other countries of the Eastern Europe and Baltics that became NATO members after the collapse of the USSR. Of course, Putin’s invasion of Ukraine has nothing to do with NATO. Ukraine wasn’t even close to becoming a member of NATO in February 2022, when Russian troops crossed the Ukrainian border. In 2.5 years of the war, Putin’s politicians and propagandists dropped most of these presences — they no longer are trying to claim that “they are liberating Ukrainians” or that they “don’t hit civilian targets”. Now, they are openly saying it’s all about annexing more land (claiming “it’s Russian historical lands”, “we are taking back what’s ours”). Any hits on civilian targets Putin’s propagandists announce “a strike on a NATO warehouse” or “the place where NATO soldiers were located”. They don’t care anymore that no one believes them. They are brazen in their arrogance: “And what will you do?” The claim “it’s our historic lands” goes well beyond Ukraine, with Putin stating that Russia is the USSR and the Russian empire, and repeating that “Russian interests must be respected”. It is only Ukraine's courageous resistance that gave Europe time to prepare for what Putin has planned for it. Already in spring 2022, Putin was planning to take over Moldova, immediately after the fall of Ukraine — which Putin was confident would be completed by the end of March 2022. Russia wages non-stop hybrid war against the NATO countries and is already escalating these activities into open acts of sabotage, endangering people’s lives. The sooner Putin is stopped and decisively beaten in Ukraine, the lower will be threat to the countries of the Eastern Europe — and the European Union as a whole.

Do you think it is fair to call a westerner who supports Putin’s invasion and actively spreads Putinist propaganda in comment sections, a quisling? Well, Moldova aren’t just calling the citizens who spread Putin’s propaganda a “quisling” (“traitor”) — they are amending the criminal code to prosecute spreading disinformation in the interests of other states as treason. The term “quisling” arose because in World War II, Vidkun Quisling, a Norwegian politician, volunteered to help the occupying Nazis rule Norway for Germany. Now the term is used to mean a traitor, especially one who collaborates with an enemy occupying force for personal gain. Quisling was arrested and tried for war crimes in 1945, and sentenced to death. He was executed on October 24, 1945. The parliamentary majority (PAS party of Moldova President Maia Sandu) proposed to expand the legal definition treason by adding another type of activity: “assisting a foreign state, foreign organization, anti-constitutional entity or their representatives to carry out hostile activities against the security of the state”. This would include, in particular, “carrying out disinformation campaigns, organized activities aimed at achieving hostile goals through disinformation, which may harm the sovereignty, independence, unity, indivisibility, security or defense capacity of the Republic of Moldova.” Russia is de-facto occupying 17% of the territory of Moldova — the areas called Transnistria and Gagauzia, since 1990s. Russia claims that Moldova violates the rights of the Russian population of these self-proclaimed “republics” (you probably never knew about their existence until today). Sounds familiar?

Are there any specific stories within the 100 Ukrainians released from Russian captivity that you found particularly moving? Here is this story that I cried reading. You might cry, too. A guy tells his mother after being released from captivity: “We didn’t believe in the exchange until the very end. Because they deceived us so much, they tormented us... They would take us for executions and for exchanges... And then they would bring us back and laugh at us. And when a soldier came into the bus and said, "You’re home, boys, Glory to Ukraine!" - I just started breathing; I hadn't been breathing, Mom, really. And when we saw people along the road greeting us with flags, flowers, and signs, it felt like a movie, like it wasn’t happening to us. And then, when we finally arrived, the first cigarette, hugs, they gave us a phone, I forgot your number, Mom, can you imagine? But you’re not mad, because how could I forget your number? I repeated it to myself for 2 years. Like you taught me in childhood - "My name is...., I live at..., Mom’s phone number is...." The boys cried, but I didn't. And at the hospital, they gave us clothes and took us to the dining room. And there was food, Mom. There were 3 bowls of different things for each of us. I don’t know, I didn’t eat that much in captivity in a month. And the smell of the soup. My head started spinning. The bowl was so deep, the soup was up to the brim. I was so careful with the spoon, trying not to spill anything, but my hands were shaking, Mom, because I wanted to eat properly, but I also wanted to just grab the bowl and drink it all. And my hands were shaking. And oh, how much I wanted to eat, you can’t imagine. And I was so careful, trying to be proper... A lady walked around, refilling everything for us, she came up to me, hugged me, stroked my head like Grandma used to, kissed me on the temple - "Eat, dear, I’ll bring more," she said. And that’s when I cried. I ate and cried, afraid to look up because I felt ashamed. And then I looked around, and almost all of us were like that - eating and crying. And the soup, Mom, I’ve never had anything tastier in my life. You’re not upset, are you, Mom?”

What can we learn from the region around Kursk, scene of a famous Soviet counter-offensive in 1943, to understand the scale of the disaster inflicted on Russia by Vladimir Putin? Russia-Ukraine war is full of symbols. Startling success of Ukraine’s offensive in the Kursk region — the scene of 1943 milestone battle of the WW2, where the Soviet army trashed Nazi troops — is one of such omens. Some western speakers make an obtuse mistake when talking about “Russia defeating Hitler” in WW2 — it wasn’t Russia but the Soviet Union. To understand the difference, bear in mind that when the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, more Soviet citizens were living outside Russia, than in Russia itself. By the same token, the Soviet effort against Nazi troops in WW2 also included more non-Russians than Russians. The second largest republic of the USSR was Ukraine — which was nearly fully occupied by Hitler in WW2, so the 7 millions Ukrainians in the Soviet Army really fought for the right to return to their homes. 1943 Battle of Kursk was the largest tank battle in history. It involved 6,000 tanks, 2,000,000 troops, and 4,000 aircraft. The USSR had 3,600 tanks, which was only made possible because of massive material support from the USA and UK. Without the American ‘Lend Lease’, the Soviet army wouldn’t be able to function at the level it needed to be. The Kursk battle dealt a final blow to German forces on the eastern front and decisively turned the tide of World War 2. Hitler troops lost the initiative, which they have never regained. So, the Kursk battle in WW2 was a turning point when the Nazis lost so badly, they never managed to recover. Soviets were proud of the Kursk battle (“Kursk Curve” in the Soviet history books). But for Vladimir Putin, the word “Kursk” is anything but pleasant. On August 12, 2000, Russian submarine “Kursk” sank, with Putin’s government screwing up the rescue effort, and all survivors aboard ending up dead. The people were especially shocked by the fact that Putin refused to return from his Black Sea vacation as the catastrophe was unfolding. On August 12, 2024, as the Ukrainian offensive in the Kursk region was progressing, president Zelenskyy said: ”We see how Russia really moves in the times of Putin: 24 years ago, there was the Kursk disaster – the symbolic beginning of his rule; and now we can see what the end for him is. And that is Kursk as well.” For superstitious Putin, the 2nd Kursk disaster must be petrifying — Putin certainly didn’t look confident at the latest briefing of Russia’s Security Council. For a long time, Putin was bragging about “Russia’s victory against Hitler”, completely denying credit to the allies (the U.S., UK, and others) and the input of other Soviet republics, including Ukraine. This time, Ukraine, backed by its allies (the U.S., UK, and others) is standing against fascist Russia — and the battlefield is once again in Kursk. This moment, no doubt, will be one of the focal points of the Russia-Ukraine war in future history books.

How significant is the joint statement signed by over 80 countries and international entities at the Global Peace Summit initiated by Ukraine in Switzerland on 15-16 June? The global peace summit in Switzerland became a major diplomatic success for Ukraine and president Zelenskyy — and therefore, a major diplomatic failure for Russia and Vladimir Putin. “The ongoing war of the Russian Federation against Ukraine continues to cause large-scale human suffering and destruction, and to create risks and crises with global repercussions for the world,” starts the joint statement. These key points are: Previously, 53 countries were supporting Ukraine in Ramstein format and contributing to its defence against the Russian invasion. Swiss Peace Summit showed that there are 27 more countries that stand with Ukraine. Definitely a slap in Putin’s face, after his pathetic ultimatum, “just give me your land, because we have utterly failed to take it by force”.

Is Russia’s talk of Ukraine using a dirty bomb on its own territory indicate that Russia may be planning to use a dirty bomb themselves and blame it on Ukraine? ‘Russia Today’, TASS, and RIA Novosti, as well as all the Putin’s shills are posting and reposting each other, threatening that “Ukraine is going to blow a dirty bomb in Eastern Europe.” Is Russia going to blow a dirty bomb somewhere and blame it on Ukraine? How did Putin handle the Kursk submarine disaster? The explosions were so powerful that they got picked by seismographs across the globe. The nearby 28,000-ton battlecruiser ‘Pyotr Velikiy’ shook from the 1st explosion. However, the Russian Navy didn’t acknowledge they had a major catastrophe. All 118 crew members aboard ‘Kursk’ perished, although 23 sailors survived the explosions and were alive for hours, hoping to be rescued. One of the ship’s officers, Lieutenant Captain Dmitri Koselnikov, left a note dated 2 hours after the 2nd explosion, saying there were 23 survivors. The submarine sank to the sea floor. The survivors barricaded themselves in a rear compartment and waited for a rescue. The rescue never came. ”Kursk”, a movie based on the disaster, starring Colin Firth, came out in 2018. As the disaster was unfolding, Vladimir Putin, the newly inaugurated president of Russia, continued his holidays on the Black Sea. Putin’s first statement about the submarine disaster was only made a week after. It took a week before a permission was granted to foreign countries to attempt a recovery mission (the Russian Navy failed to get into the sunk submarine) — and on August 21, a team of British and Norwegian divers accessed the vessel and found its entire crew dead. In 2000, the Russian media was still privately owned, so the coverage of how the Russian state handled the ‘Kursk’ disaster was sharply critical. Putin was furious over the ways TV amplified his haphazard response. He accused the TV producers in “hiring $10 whores” to pose as wives of deceased sailors, with the goal to portray him, Vladimir Putin, in a bad light. Kursk’s commanding officer, Gennady Lyachin; photo from 1999 parade. When questioned by relatives of the deceased on August 22, 2000, Putin put the blame on Russia’s “economic and military decline” before he came to power. It’s unlikely that there will be many mentions of the sunk ‘Kursk’ in the Russian media today. Not when Russia just suffered such a humiliating invasion by Ukraine last week, precisely in the Kursk region.

Why did Muscovy change its name to Russia? ”Russia” is the English word; in reality, the name of the state that Muscovy principality decided to adopt as the name of its empire was “Rossia”. “Rossia” is the Greek word for “Rus” — the name of the historical Slavic state with the capital in Kyiv. The USSR historians began calling it “Kievan Rus”, because in the Soviet history books the history of the USSR was starting with 9th century Rus. The legend of Kyiv being founded in 482 by brothers Kyi, Shchek, Khoryv and their sister Lybid was also included. By adopting the name “Rossia” (Russia) Muscovy princes laid their claim on the lands that belonged to Ukraine. 1709 newspaper “The Daily Courant” talks about Muscovy and Ukraine. The decision to change the name from the principality of Muscovy to the Russian Empire was political, and, as it was customary at the time, accompanied by forged history, backing the claim. In our times, Vladimir Putin, the ruler of the Russian Federation, is also forging history, trying to lay claim on the territories outside of the internationally recognized Russia’s borders. 17th century thinking in the 21st century. Insane.
